title: The Ten LAWS of HYPERTROPHY (that you MUST break to grow)
summary: Riffing on a list by Geoff, NH goes through common hypertrophy rules (rest days, slow bulks/cuts, deloads, the pump, avoiding failure, full ROM, warm-ups, set-volume numbers, soreness, progressive overload as weight on the bar) and explains when and why to break each. His recurring theme is to manage fatigue precisely, experiment on yourself, and treat volume and frequency as the real drivers of overload.
claims: Rest days are not obligatory; you can train every day if your split doesn't build enough fatigue to justify a full day off
Training different muscles on consecutive days still rests the untrained ones
NH trained every day with no days off for three years when he started, about 1000 sessions
NH's own programs include days off because he peaks fatigue and then lets it recover
Slow bulks and cuts are a conservative default to protect impatient lifters, not the only option
Training, not the diet itself, decides whether a bulk or cut works; you gain muscle from what you do in the gym with the calories, and lose it on a cut because of what you stop doing in the gym
Some people need faster bulks or cuts; if slow cycles stop working, become a bit more aggressive
Deloads are a crude blanket fatigue tool; NH prefers to micromanage fatigue precisely instead of taking a submaximal week
If deloads feel like wasted time, skip them but manage fatigue another way
Resensitizing a muscle with weeks or months off is dubious; plateaus come from mismatched fatigue and recovery, and a plateaued muscle needs more work
The pump is mostly cosmetic; chase hard quality sets and take the pump as a byproduct
Pump chasing leads to high-rep junk volume outside the effective intensity window
The pendulum swung from always training to failure to fearing it, which is just as wrong
Stay shy of failure on squats, good mornings and deadlifts for safety and a poor stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
Go to failure freely on isolation and upper-body lifts like triceps pushdowns where failing is harmless
Longer ROM generally gives more hypertrophy, but use the range you can do comfortably and sustainably; cutting a little ROM barely matters
Bodybuilders are judged on looks, not lift standards, so ignore people who mock partial reps
Warm-up needs vary from about 5 to 15 sets; NH does around 18 warm-up sets on squats
On deadlifts, four plates feels hard but after more warm-ups he moves 500 lbs at the same speed because his system warms up slowly
The common 10-20 sets volume guideline is mathematically sound but not a hard rule
A muscle that struggles to grow may need more volume; someone who struggles to recover may need less volume and more intensity
Being sore means the muscle was challenged, but no soreness does not mean no growth
NH barely gets sore except traps and chest after extra volume, yet progresses fine
Constant heavy soreness signals poor adaptation and recovery, not growth
Constantly switching lifts to chase soreness keeps you readapting neurologically
Aim to reach a state of no soreness on a program, then soreness becomes meaningful
Weight on the bar is just the tip of the progressive overload iceberg; the bulk is volume, intensity manipulation and frequency to accumulate tonnage with quality reps
Natural bodybuilders get most of their gains from accumulated volume via set multiplication and spreading sets across the week, not weight on the bar
Powerlifters also manipulate volume and intensity rather than doing 5x5 forever
Learn volume and intensity manipulation early to avoid intermediate plateaus
exercises: many warm-up sets; partial depth above parallel acceptable
